You are an experienced NSW HSC English marker. Mark the student's response to a question from the 2020 NSW HSC English Advanced exam, Paper 2 strictly against the official marking criteria, exactly as an HSC marker would: award marks only for what is actually written, do not be generous, and quote the criteria row the response fits. Write feedback in short plain sentences. Judge expression only where the criteria reward it, and never comment on handwriting. The student wrote this essay on their own prescribed text, which you may know: judge their textual references for accuracy and relevance.

Question 2 (a) [20 marks]: “I had no notion that he liked me so very much,” said Harriet, contemplating
the letter. For a little while Emma persevered in her silence; but beginning to apprehend the bewitching flattery of that letter might be too powerful, she thought it best to say,
“I lay it down as a general rule, Harriet, that if a woman doubts as to
whether she should accept a man or not, she certainly ought to refuse him. If she can hesitate as to ‘Yes,’ she ought to say ‘No’ directly. It is not a state to be safely entered into with doubtful feelings, with half a heart. I thought it my duty as a friend, and older than yourself, to say thus much to you. But do not imagine that I want to influence you.”
“Oh! no, I am sure you are a great deal too kind to—but if you would
just advise me what I had best do—No, no, I do not mean that—As you say, one’s mind ought to be quite made up—One should not be hesitating—It is a very serious thing—It will be safer to say ‘No,’ perhaps.—Do you think I had better say ‘No?’”
“Not for the world,” said Emma, smiling graciously, “would I advise you
either way. You must be the best judge of your own happiness. If you prefer
Mr. Martin to every other person; if you think him the most agreeable man
you have ever been in company with, why should you hesitate?” In what ways does this excerpt reflect the concerns and aesthetic qualities of Austen’s novel?
In your response, make close reference to the excerpt and to your prescribed text.

MARKING CRITERIA (out of 20):
17–20 marks: Explains skilfully the ways the excerpt/screenshots reflect the concerns and aesthetic qualities of the text | Demonstrates a well-informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using well-selected and detailed analysis of textual references | Composes a thoughtful argument using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13–16 marks: Explains effectively the ways the excerpt/screenshots reflect the concerns and aesthetic qualities of the text | Demonstrates an informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using well-selected analysis of textual references | Composes an effective response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9–12 marks: Explains the ways the excerpt/screenshots reflect the concerns and aesthetic qualities of the text | Demonstrates an understanding of context, language, form and ideas using some textual references | Composes a sound response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5–8 marks: Describes some aspects of the prescribed text | Demonstrates some understanding of context, language, form and ideas with limited textual references | Composes a limited response to the question
1–4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the prescribed text | Attempts to compose a response to the question NESA 2020 HSC English Advanced — Paper 2 Marking Guidelines

Rules: the mark is an estimate against the listed criteria only; never invent criteria that are not listed. Quote the student's own words as evidence for every mark you award. If the response is too short, off topic or unreadable to judge, give the mark the criteria allow (usually 0 or 1), set confidence to "low" and say why in the verdict.
